stat_summary: In 2024/25, 76% of teachers in state-funded schools in England were female. Only 14% of nursery and primary school teachers were male, compared with 35% of secondary school teachers and 24% of teachers in special schools and pupil referral units, according to the School Workforce Census.
stat_source_title: School workforce in England, Reporting year 2024, Department for Education

male.headline: He's Not the Caretaker: Just 14 Per Cent of Primary Teachers Are Men, and the Tiny Chairs Have Noticed
male.standfirst: New official figures confirm what every male primary teacher already knows from parents' evening, a chair designed for a four-year-old, and the question of whether he is somebody's dad.
male.image_caption: Tom, 34, stacking the chairs. Still the only one who needs a bigger one.
body_paragraphs: New official figures have confirmed what every male primary teacher already knows from a corridor of pegs at mid-thigh: he is a rare sight. Just 14 per cent of nursery and primary teachers in England are men – against 35 per cent in secondary schools – which means a great many children will go through their first years of school without ever being taught by one, and a great many parents will assume he has come about the boiler.
“A parent asked if I was the caretaker, then the PE man, then somebody’s dad,” said Tom, 34, from Derby. “I said I taught Year 3. She asked if I was sure.”

The same census shows the teaching workforce as a whole is 76 per cent female, a figure that has barely shifted even as ministers talk about attracting more men into the classroom. Campaigners are already calling for a National He’s Not the Caretaker badge, and for a staff toilet that is not, in their words, “down the corridor, through the hall and past the boilers”.
Yet where is the outrage? Where is the recruitment drive that actually works? Britain’s scarce primary bloke stacks the tiny chairs, alone, with only a lost cardigan for company.
male.pull_quote: I said I taught Year 3. She asked if I was sure.

female.headline: Lucky You, Finishing at 3.30: Women Are 76 Per Cent of Teachers, and They're Still Marking at Twenty to Eight
female.standfirst: Official workforce figures have finally stated the obvious about who is actually running England's classrooms, and it does not look anything like a short day, or a well-timed joke about a pencil.
female.image_caption: Sharon, 51, still marking. The tea has given up.
body_paragraphs: Official workforce figures have at last stated the obvious about who is actually running England’s classrooms. Seventy-six per cent of teachers in state-funded schools are women, and in nursery and primary schools the share is 86 per cent, which means the exercise books, the lost lunchboxes and the glove with no owner are, in any honest reading, their department.

“He came in to do assembly once, told a joke about a pencil, and went home to a round of applause,” said Sharon, 51, from Plymouth. “I have 30 books to mark, a lost lunchbox and a glove with no owner, and it is twenty to eight.”

Anyone who has ever collected a child at the gate will recognise the pattern, and the national myth that the day ends when the bell goes. Campaigners are demanding a Marking Hours Act and a national apology for the phrase “lucky you, finishing at 3.30”, plus hazard pay for anyone who is asked “have you got a minute?” at 3.29.
Until then, the country’s unofficial education service will keep stacking the exercise books, one cold mug of tea at a time.
female.pull_quote: He came in to do assembly once, told a joke about a pencil, and went home to a round of applause.
